title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
abstract: When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default. For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content. Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI , an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source. In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation. This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova. Solution overview Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler when it can reach and index the pages you need. It respects robots.txt , and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content. Use the Crawl4AI preparation path when public source material needs one or more of the following before ingestion: Structured Markdown preparation : Use DefaultMarkdownGenerator with a pruning content filter to reduce navigation and other boilerplate while preserving headings, lists, and tables. Because pruning is heuristic, review representative output from your sites. Bounded, targeted extraction : Extract only the page region that an optional CSS selector matches. Constrain breadth-first traversal by seed origin, page/path/host scope, depth and page caps, and URL patterns. Custom metadata : Attach source URLs, crawl timestamps, content type, and your own attributes to each document, so that you can filter retrieval results on them. Because managed and customer-managed knowledge bases both support Amazon S3 data sources, the Crawl4AI path works with either type. This post uses a managed knowledge base and notes where a customer-managed knowledge base differs. The rest of this post follows the companion sample. Treat its architecture and defaults as a starting point, not as requirements of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. By default, the sample runs the AWS Fargate task in a public subnet, where it reaches your configured websites through an internet gateway. Crawl4AI’s role ends once it has prepared the source documents and metadata sidecars. From ingestion onward, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval. title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping. One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost. In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI . We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark. Figure 1: One agentic task is a loop, not a single call: the agent searches, reads results, refines, verifies, and decides, and each step is a separate billed call to the frontier model. A single completed task can be multiple calls, on every shopper What is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD)? The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text , with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as logit-based or on-policy, it sits at the most cost-effective and portable end of the distillation spectrum. The teacher writes the answers, and the student is fine-tuned on them. Because those answers persist as a dataset, you can reuse them to train or test different students without regenerating the data. In principle, you would want the student to match the teacher’s full distribution over possible outputs. The caveat here is that you can’t. The space of possible sequences is astronomically large, so matching it exactly isn’t feasible. SeqKD sidesteps that by approximating it with samples the teacher actually produces. For an agent, the sequence the teacher produces is not a block of prose but a trajectory, an ordered run of reasoning, tool calls, and the observations they return, where each step is conditioned on everything before it. Training the student on that whole sequence teaches it the reasoning that leads to each action and the multi-step course of action itself, not a single paragraph of answer text. That makes an agentic task one of the cleanest illustrations of sequence-level KD, because the sequence being copied is the behavior itself. title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check. A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment. In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , and the open source Strands Agents SDK . A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own. Solution overview The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead. Three pillars define the architecture: Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review. Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more than one specialist contributed. Complex questions such as “Check if this wheel is going end-of-life, find alternatives, and score them” chain all three specialists in sequence. Human-in-the-loop decision – The system drafts justification memos and Integration Impact Assessments for engineering review, but it doesn’t recommend or approve a substitution. Every evaluation also writes an audit trail entry aligned with AS9100 sections 8.4 and 8.5.6. The following diagram shows the architecture. Figure 1: Architecture of the multi-agent engineering assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. In this solution, chat requests from the engineer’s application flow into a multi-agent graph hosted on AgentCore runtime: a planner (Claude Haiku 5.5) produces a routing plan, specialists (Claude Sonnet 5.5) execute their tools, and a supervisor (Claude Opus 5.5) synthesizes their results when more than one specialist ran. The specialists retrieve from a managed knowledge base that we created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through an AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, alongside the Web Search connector for live web data. For image-as-query (uploading a chart to identify a part), the agent calls a native Amazon S3 Vectors index directly, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input. title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
abstract: This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K. Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin. At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin. To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock , a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened. Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics. In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and share lessons learned from scaling the system. The challenge of triage overhead Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context. When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch , examining application-level traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service , checking Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task status, and cross-referencing symptoms with internal runbooks in GitHub. This gave engineers the information they needed, but it also showed how much repetitive context gathering would be required as more services were onboarded. The team recognized two areas where a proactive investment could help. First, the same log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups would be repeated for every incident. Second, the depth and speed of triage could vary with the on-call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service. As alert volume and service ownership grew, switching between multiple tools for each investigation could slow response and make it harder to apply the team’s best practices consistently. Circle K’s DevOps team therefore started a research and development (R&D) initiative to explore how AI could support monitoring and incident triage. The goal was to automate repetitive context gathering and provide structured, actionable findings, while supporting engineers’ operational judgment during an investigation. Why Circle K chose Amazon Bedrock The team evaluated several approaches before building, including open source agent frameworks on self-managed infrastructure. That approach would have meant owning model hosting, prompt versioning, tool orchestration, and security controls. With Amazon Bedrock, the team avoided that overhead. The Monday Morning Agent: Defining the Tush Push
abstract: “Tush push” never appears in our roughly 265,000 play descriptions from 2021 through the current season. Neither does “brotherly shove,” and “sneak” turns up only twice. So when we asked our AI analyst to tackle “Ban the Tush Push” in the October 26 episode of The Monday Morning Agent , we first had to define the play using the available data. We saved that definition in a shared data dictionary, the agent’s first durable memory, so future runs must use the same definition and explain its limitations. Check whether the data supports your definition A quarterback takes the snap, and teammates push him forward. Our data identifies the ball carrier but doesn’t record whether teammates pushed him. We can check whether a snap came from shotgun, but we can’t reconstruct the team’s specific formation. We explored five possible definitions, from a quarterback sneak with teammates pushing to any rush on third or fourth and short. Each definition changes which plays the analysis counts. The broadest one would count running backs too, which takes us away from the play people are arguing about. So before you let an agent query a term everyone seems to understand, write its definition in plain language. Then go clause by clause and ask whether the data can support it. A familiar name doesn’t guarantee a usable label. Write down what your definition can’t measure We settled on a quarterback run with one yard or less to go, from under center. The agent counts qualifying quarterback sneaks whether anyone pushes the runner or not. We’re measuring a substitute for the tush push, and we can’t isolate the shove’s contribution. Even “quarterback” needs a definition. The fields available to our tool don’t include player position, so the tool identifies the quarterback as the player who threw the most passes for that team in that game. That’s another assumption to check when you interpret the results. The dictionary entry has to explain the play in plain language and state what the data can’t tell us. Otherwise, readers could assume a “tush push” result counts plays with a push. Keep the limitation beside the definition so the agent can repeat it with the result. Give the next run the same definition The dictionary holds one JSON file per definition, with a fixed structure. The agent can add an entry, but it can’t change an existing one. A different definition needs a new name. That keeps the meaning attached to an earlier result from quietly changing later. Before each run, the script that launches the agent, called the runner, saves a copy of the dictionary and adds its contents to the agent’s instructions with the date. The agent searches for an existing definition first. If it finds one, it uses it. If it doesn’t, it can write a new entry using the fields the tool supports. In the demonstration, the tool refused the request for “tush push” because no entry existed. The agent then created a definition and queried it. Check that the agent uses its memory Writing “use the dictionary” in a policy doesn’t make the agent obey. We’re building this around instruction, check, and enforcement. The policy tells the agent to use and cite an entry. The tool accepts definitions from the dictionary rather than a definition improvised in a query. If the answer lacks the required ruling, the runner retries once, then stops if it’s still missing. We expanded the agent’s permissions to let it add a dictionary entry alongside querying the plays. Test whether your agent uses its shared definitions and whether someone reading the answer can find them. Read the conversion rate before deciding on a ban Across five complete seasons, the defined play converted 78.3% of the time, compared with 70% for other short-yardage rushes. That’s an 8.3 percentage point advantage. While the agent found an advantage, it didn’t treat the conversion gap as sufficient evidence for a ban. title: Practical Loop Engineering
abstract: The following article originally appeared on Addy Osmani’s Elevate blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. The way that I typically work is I have anywhere between five and ten agents working at the same time in parallel. There are going to be some tasks that I’m very happy to delegate fully to agents, as long as I have a very clear idea of the stopping conditions and the constraints around them. And then there are going to be some tasks where I am going to want to keep a closer eye on and code-review what the agent is doing. You’ve probably heard about loop engineering . I talked about it a couple of months ago when I wrote a big blog post about it. A loop is an autonomous, self-correcting feedback cycle where an AI agent repeatedly acts, tests its results, and adjusts its approach until a specific goal is met. There are now basically two core primitives you can think about. In Claude Code you have a goal primitive , which can drive a single bounded task forward until you’ve got a particular goal, like a measurable finish line that’s been met. And then loop reruns on a timer or a fixed interval, so you can use it to schedule changes. Before the primitives were primitives I remember back before we had primitives baked into Claude Code and Codex: Loop engineering was heavily about setting up your own bash loop, a hand-rolled thing. That’s how I approached it. And you might remember earlier in the year, a number of us were playing around with the Ralph loop by Geoff Huntley. We were experimenting, we were sharing our workflows, we were sharing what worked and what didn’t, but it was largely on some of our personal projects where, if we ran into a wall, it didn’t really have a big cost to us. And as we’ve tried to see what patterns and what aspects of loop engineering are now a little bit more baked, I think we have a clearer idea of how you babysit it. I can now largely rely on the output of the primitives in Claude Code and Codex. We’ve come a little way. But at the same time we need to be very diligent, because loop engineering, where you kind of leave it sitting alone and haven’t really thought about whether the end goal or the constraints have been well defined, can leave you in a problematic state. This is why there’s nuance when deciding to use it for an evergreen codebase without users or without as much historical complexity as a brownfield bank codebase. How the Claude Code team frames loops The Claude Code team published their take on four kinds of loops, and it lines up with how I use the primitives ( their write-up ). Before we get to it, here’s my quick summary: On the Claude Code team, we define loops as agents repeating cycles of work until a stop condition is met. We categorize a few different types of loops based on how they are triggered, how they are stopped, what Claude Code primitive is used, what type of task is most appropriate for each. Not all tasks require complex loops; start with the simplest solution and use these patterns selectively. Every prompt you send starts a manual loop with you directing each turn. Claude gathers context, takes action, checks its work, repeats if needed, and responds. We call this the agentic loop. For example, ask Claude to create a “Like” button. It reads your code, makes the edit, runs the tests, and hands back something it believes works. You then manually check the work, and write the next prompt. Their write-up walks each rung. On goal-based loops: Sometimes, a single turn is not enough, especially for more complex tasks. Agents do better when they can iterate. You can extend how long Claude keeps iterating by defining what done looks like with /goal. When you define the success criteria, Claude doesn’t have to make a determination on what is “good enough” and end the loop early. title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
abstract: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses. Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights. Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context. Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive. Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents. title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
abstract: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. title: The agentic web is here
abstract: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus. They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight. As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
abstract: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “ I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper ,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses. “He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.” Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it. Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions , Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools. “Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.” If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty . Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity. Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

title: Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights
abstract: It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light. Why large dogs age faster In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called "jumping genes," according to a paper published in the journal Science. The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It's part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation. Read full article Comments

title: Third person dies of bird flu since virus started jumping to livestock
abstract: A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday . It marks the third human bird flu death in the US since a strain of highly pathogenic (H5) avian influenza (HPAI) made the unprecedented jump from wild, migratory birds to dairy cows, which was first reported in the US in March 2024 . The person who died was a Yakima County resident and was said to have had underlying health conditions, which could have made the person more vulnerable to the infection. On Friday, county officials reported that the person was severely ill and hospitalized . In the subsequent announcement of the person's death, officials said they would not be releasing further information about the person, including their name, gender, or age, out of respect for the family's privacy. "Our hearts go out to the individual's family and loved ones during this difficult time," Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. "Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low." Read full article Comments

title: Googling "Zelda" today offers a glimpse of how search worked in 1998
abstract: The year was 1998. Britney Spears topped the charts, Bill Clinton was impeached, and a couple of little websites called Google and Ars Technica came online. It was also the year Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. Google, which has come to dominate the Internet (Ars is still working on that), is celebrating the imminent release of the Ocarina of Time remaster by temporarily transporting us back to that storied year with a search Easter egg. To access the Google time machine, you just have to search for either "Zelda" or "Ocarina of Time." Google will load the standard 2026 results page, but you'll see an animated Master Sword in the lower right corner. It appears on both mobile and desktop—just click the sword and enjoy the show. After a little time-skipping animation and a Link shout (you know the one), you'll swear it's 1998 again. The search page is transformed into a simple list of blue links with retro Google branding. This is particularly apt given the time-shifting mechanics in Ocarina of Time . Read full article Comments

title: Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree
abstract: It's widely acknowledged that it's nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. "We didn't see anything" is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore. The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don't seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don't have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy. Inconsistencies One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in "cognitive reappraisal." This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience. Read full article Comments

title: Claude’s new rules against game cloning won’t stop the AI copying boom
abstract: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it's unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months. A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name "chasm" was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name "tengu_heron_brook"—reads as follows: Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original. XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30 . XDA also reported that the "tengu_heron_brook" rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle. title: F1 in Mexico City: Yet another Ferrari fiasco, but that’s not all
abstract: Formula 1 has a new World Drivers' Champion. Just a few months after turning 20, Kimi Antonelli sealed his first title this weekend at Mexico City, becoming the sport’s youngest-ever champion. Elsewhere, there was drama aplenty, perhaps a consequence of the thin air affecting decision-making in some cases. The race was Ferrari’s to win, but yet again, the team handed victory to a rival this season, in this case Red Bull. Further down the grid, we saw a last-minute driver change in the Haas team, synchronized retirements from both Aston Martins, and the wheels literally coming off Cadillac Racing. And there was I, expecting a dull weekend. It might not be as high as Pikes Peak , but at an elevation of 7,350 feet (2,240 m) above sea level, the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez provides a unique challenge on the F1 calendar. Wings that would create huge amounts of downforce at circuits like Monaco just generate Monza-like levels in Mexico, and there’s little slipstream effect when following another car. Cooling tends to be a problem, too, with insufficient airflow across radiators, and obviously engine power is reduced with less oxygen to burn. The track is very flat, with a rather low-grip surface and mostly medium- and slow-speed corners, including a processional route through a stadium that was built in the 1990s, plus a very long run from the start into turn 1. title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
abstract: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling where the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans. A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass. Clockwork compass Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales. Read full article Comments

title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
abstract: In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies? Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.” At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects. title: Roz: A Taste Test for World Model Latents
abstract: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.

title: Dataset Mismatch Matters in Group Relative Policy Optimization for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
abstract: Recently, reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is practically very important, where the leading approach is group relative policy optimization (GRPO) that typically faces a trade-off between rollout efficiency and downstream performance. To improve efficiency while preserving performance, existing selective rollout methods mainly exploit only source-side training dynamics to optimize the discrete distribution over source prompts. However, in practice, the source training dataset is rarely identically distributed to the target test dataset. When such a mismatch exists, due to legal or privacy constraints, it is usually not acceptable to share target prompts themselves with the RLVR trainer. Nevertheless, it is still possible for the target data owner to provide limited aggregated feedback from a small held-out target set without revealing target prompts or rollout traces. In this paper, we propose learning-to-reweight rollout (L2RR) that explicitly incorporates target-side performance feedback into GRPO. Specifically, L2RR learns a discrete sampling distribution over source prompts by optimizing a bi-level objective that maximizes accuracy on a held-out target dataset, while simultaneously penalizing rollouts that provide little incremental learning information. Empirical studies on six math reasoning benchmarks and three model scales show that L2RR improves target-domain performance and increases rollout efficiency.

title: ECG2Gene: Deep Learning-Based Germline Tumor Susceptibility Gene Risk Assessment Using Electrocardiograms
abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) may contain physiological information related to hereditary cancer susceptibility, but its relationship with future cancer risk remains unclear. Here, we present ECG2Gene, a two-stage deep-learning framework that derives digital phenotypes related to germline tumor susceptibility from routine 12-lead ECGs and predicts future cancer risk. In Stage 1, carrier status for pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in ATM, BRIP1, CHEK2, PALB2, BRCA1, and BRCA2 supervises a multitask model that generates six continuous ECG-derived gene scores. In Stage 2, XGBoost integrates these scores with clinical variables to predict subsequent breast and ovarian cancer in women and prostate cancer in men. We also introduce ECG-Wide Association Analysis (EWAS) to characterize associations between ECG-derived gene scores and ECG waveforms. Across the clinical feature combinations evaluated in UK Biobank, the best-performing sex-specific models achieve AUROCs of 0.683, 0.633, and 0.660 for breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer, respectively. In external evaluations, models combining ECG-derived gene scores with age achieve prostate cancer AUROCs of 0.709 and 0.579 among men in the overall China Kadoorie Biobank and MIMIC-IV-ECG cohorts, respectively. ECG2Gene links genetically supervised ECG phenotyping and waveform association analysis to future cancer outcomes, demonstrating the potential of routine ECGs combined with clinical information for non-invasive, opportunistic cancer risk assessment.

title: Sharp Design-based Inference for Quantiles of Individual Treatment Effects
abstract: Understanding the distribution of individual treatment effects (ITEs) is a central problem in causal inference. In general, however, this distribution is only partially identifiable from observed data because it depends on the unidentifiable joint distribution of the two potential outcomes. In this paper, we develop design-based inference for the distribution of ITEs whose validity relies solely on the randomization of treatment assignment, treating the potential outcomes as arbitrary fixed constants. Building on recent randomization tests for ITE quantiles, we propose tests based on either a rank-based Kolmogorov--Smirnov (KS) statistic or the usual KS statistic, with the latter being more conservative in the presence of ties. We show that, under certain regularity conditions, the confidence bounds obtained by test inversion are asymptotically no worse than the sharp bounds on ITE quantiles given the marginal distributions of the potential outcomes. We further derive a closed-form expression for the confidence bounds from the KS-based randomization test and show that they can be equivalently constructed by combining sharp bounds on ITE quantiles with uncertainty of empirical marginal distributions. This equivalence connects randomization-based inference with partial identification and clarifies the special role of the KS statistic in achieving sharp inference. Under additional distributional assumptions, we characterize the power of the proposed randomization tests under local alternatives. Finally, we discuss how to incorporate covariates to further sharpen inference. We illustrate the properties of the proposed methods using both simulations and a real-data application.

title: Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards: Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer
abstract: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.

title: ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive (AR) language models by letting a small model draft tokens serially and a large model verify them in parallel. We reverse these roles. Starting from a standard AR checkpoint, we fine-tune the large model into a proposer that predicts a block of future tokens in a single forward pass, then use one additional forward pass to verify the proposed block. This gives ProVe, Proposer-Verifier decoding. The verifier can be a smaller AR model or the proposer itself; the latter gives ProVe-lossless, which reproduces the proposer's greedy AR decoding. Block proposals already provide substantial room for acceleration: with a block size of 16, the proposed block has an average AR-matching prefix of 6.6 tokens on GSM8K. Across six benchmarks with a 32B proposer, ProVe-lossless reaches 2.5x average AR throughput without training a separate draft head. With a small 3B verifier, ProVe reaches 2.7x average throughput at 2.6 accuracy points below AR on the six-task average, providing a controllable tradeoff between speed and accuracy.

title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
abstract: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19--23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running 24.5times faster on TREC DL and 16.7times faster on BRIGHT.

title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

title: TSFLab: A Self-Improving Agent-Agnostic Workbench for Time Series Forecasting Research
abstract: As publications and products on time series forecasting (TSF) proliferate, researchers face a growing burden of analyzing existing work. First, not all publications release code. For instance, only about 20% of arXiv TSF papers have a code link in the surveyed period. Second, released code also requires manual maintenance. Thus, TSF researchers must constantly adapt or implement existing works. However, independent implementations can differ in experimental settings and are difficult to maintain. We therefore propose to use AI agents for benchmarking TSF research and even supporting autoresearch, e.g., developing new TSF models. Yet directly applying existing coding agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, is suboptimal: prohibitive costs, limited scalability to large research projects (e.g., benchmarking), and lack of self-maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose TSFLab, a self-improving agent-agnostic "workbench" that equips compatible coding agents with shared resources and tools for low-cost TSF research and continuous maintenance of research resources. Our experiments cover reproduction, benchmarking, and new method development. In reproduction and benchmarking, TSFLab improves task completion by 20-163% and cuts fresh tokens per completed task by 11-66% across baselines. A pilot study of agent-driven method development also shows improved forecasting accuracy via TSFLab, with 32.8-73.6% fewer fresh tokens and 9.2-68.8% less development time than the other settings.

title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding
abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and τ-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.

title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
abstract: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately 3times speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/

title: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report
abstract: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.

title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
abstract: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

title: When Requirements Interact: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding via Interdependent Specifications
abstract: To succeed in real-world long-horizon software development, coding agents must satisfy multi-dimensional task specifications, such as interface compatibility and error handling, and do so without breaking existing dependencies. However, current works lack specification in both quantity and diversity, often emphasizing primary goals while ignoring complex constraints. Synthesizing tasks to bridge this gap presents two challenges: naively adding specifications risks reducing tasks to trivial checklists rather than compelling joint reasoning, and verifying these subtle interactions risks overlooking hidden flaws or rejecting valid alternatives. To address these challenges, we introduce CodeSpecWeave, a framework for synthesizing tasks with rich, interdependent specifications. Grounded in real developer seeds, a synthesis agent iteratively develops both coupled task requirements and executable tests, while a review agent audits solution trajectories from multiple models to guarantee test reliability. Using this pipeline, we construct 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. Applying Reinforcement learning on these tasks significantly improves performance over the base model on DeepSWE-v1.1, largely outperforming existing baselines. Furthermore, we curate CodeSpecWeave-Bench, a rigorous benchmark comprising 100 tasks and 1,044 specifications, which clearly separates frontier models and reveals significant headroom in handling interdependent engineering constraints.

title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling
abstract: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.

title: Supervising the Visible State: Separating Representation from View Selection in Streaming Video
abstract: An action seen once and the same action seen three times receive the same action-recognition label, so that supervision does not require a model to count. Answers shared across histories that differ in event order, accumulation, or relations leave those distinctions unconstrained; we call this state under-specification. Visible-State Supervision (ViSS) addresses it by training on source-grounded probes of event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and answer sufficiency; under the same recent-frame interface it improves OVO-Bench over a strict-matched generic temporal supervision baseline while remaining comparable on StreamingBench, with the largest gain in hallucination detection. Test-Time Causal View Search (TVS) then adapts evidence access while keeping the learned model fixed, expanding from recent frames to sparse event and compact history views on demand. The two interventions separate representation from view selection: supervision particularly benefits hallucination detection and causal reasoning, access particularly benefits event recall and forward reasoning. Together they reach the best reported accuracy among the published systems compared here on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench at a fraction of the processed frames of exhaustive selection, and strict replay shows that most of the remaining gap to a three-view oracle is a correct answer that was later replaced. Streaming accuracy depends on what supervision asks the model to keep, what evidence inference exposes, and whether the model keeps a correct answer once it has one.

title: Venus-DefakerOne2: A Vision-Forensics Foundation Model with Broader Coverage
abstract: Real-world forgery is inherently heterogeneous: it manifests not only as digital manipulation but also as physical spoofing, and is carried not only by images but also by videos. Despite substantial progress, a unified anti-forgery foundation model covering such a broad threat spectrum remains absent. In this paper, we present Venus-DefakerOne2, which substantially extends the forensic capability boundary along both the forgery-form and media-type dimensions. Trained on tens of millions of open-source and in-house samples, it incorporates two key designs. Tide-Style-Tuning alternates LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning to balance computational efficiency, generalization, and hard-sample fitting while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Entropy-based Test Adaptation determines the optimal prediction modality by analyzing prediction entropy. Venus-DefakerOne2 achieves new state-of-the-art performance across a comprehensive suite of benchmarks, including DeepFake faces (96.7%), AI-generated images (93.3%), tampered documents (87.6%), manipulated natural images (89.6%), physical spoofs (93.1%), and AI-generated videos (96.0%).
